questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Limits of real growth as a welfare measure
questions.learningObjective: Explain why rising real GDP per person may not improve welfare
questions.stem: A nation's real GDP per person rises 3% this year, yet surveys show unchanged life satisfaction; what best explains this gap?

options.text: Real GDP omits household production, leisure, and environmental quality, so gains need not raise welfare.
options.misconception: treats real GDP as a complete measure of well-being

options.text: The price index is overstated, so true growth is higher than reported.
options.misconception: confuses measurement error with a welfare gap

options.text: Inflation eroded nominal wages, leaving purchasing power unchanged.
options.misconception: confuses real with nominal income movements

options.text: Growth came entirely from longer working hours, offsetting leisure losses.
options.misconception: assumes longer hours always cancel income gains

questions.explanation: Real GDP per person captures marketed output, not leisure, home production, or environment, so it can rise without improving welfare. The tempting idea that inflation or hours fully explain the gap overstates those channels.
questions.hint: Ask what GDP leaves out of well-being.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute real output per person from aggregate data
questions.stem: Real GDP is 480 billion and population is 24 million; what is real output per person in dollars?
questions.explanation: Divide real GDP by population: 480,000,000,000 / 24,000,000 = 20,000. The value represents average marketed output per resident.
questions.hint: Divide aggregate real output by population.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the income-approach components of GDP
questions.stem: Under the income approach, GDP equals the sum of wages, rents, interest, and what fourth component?

options.text: Taxes on production, which are added without subtracting subsidies.
options.misconception: ignores the subtraction of subsidies

options.text: Profits, which include corporate and proprietor income plus inventory valuation adjustments.
options.misconception: omits inventory valuation adjustments from profits

options.text: Depreciation, which is added back to net domestic product.
options.misconception: treats depreciation as income rather than capital consumption

options.text: Consumption spending, which anchors the expenditure approach instead.
options.misconception: confuses the income approach with the expenditure approach

questions.explanation: The income approach sums wages, rents, interest, and profits (including proprietor and corporate income plus adjustments). Taxes less subsidies and depreciation relate to the bridge to national income, not the fourth primary component.
questions.hint: Think of the four factor incomes.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why nominal figures overstate real growth when prices rise
questions.stem: A team notes nominal output grew 8% while the deflator rose 5%; write a short explanation of real growth.

answer.exemplar: Real growth equals nominal growth minus inflation, roughly 3 percent, so the 8 percent nominal figure overstates true output growth once prices are stripped out.

questions.explanation: Real growth is found by deflating nominal output; with 8% nominal and 5% inflation, real growth is about 3%. The tempting 8% figure conflates price increases with volume gains.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish GDP from national income
questions.stem: Which adjustment converts GDP to national income?

options.text: Subtract indirect business taxes and add subsidies, then subtract depreciation.
options.misconception: reverses the treatment of indirect taxes and subsidies

options.text: Add net foreign factor income and subtract consumption of fixed capital.
options.misconception: double counts foreign income and capital consumption

options.text: Subtract depreciation and indirect business taxes less subsidies.
options.misconception: omits the addition of subsidies net of taxes

options.text: Subtract consumption of fixed capital and indirect business taxes, then add subsidies.
options.misconception: states the correct rule but mislabels depreciation

questions.explanation: National income equals GDP minus consumption of fixed capital minus indirect business taxes plus subsidies. Option D states this correctly; A reverses signs, B adds foreign income wrongly, C omits subsidies.
questions.hint: Remove capital consumption and net indirect taxes.

questions.learningObjective: Convert GDP to GNP using net factor income from abroad
questions.stem: GDP is 500 billion and net factor income from abroad is -10 billion; what is GNP?
questions.explanation: GNP equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad: 500 + (-10) = 490 billion. Negative net factor income means residents earn less abroad than foreigners earn domestically.
questions.hint: Add net factor income from abroad to GDP.

questions.stem: Personal income is 300 billion and personal taxes are 45 billion; what is disposable personal income?
questions.explanation: Disposable personal income equals personal income minus personal taxes: 300 - 45 = 255 billion. This is the income households can spend or save.
questions.hint: Subtract personal taxes from personal income.

questions.stem: A country's real GDP per person grew 4% while its Gini coefficient worsened; which statement best captures the welfare implication?

options.text: Growth is meaningless if inequality rises, so real GDP is useless.
options.misconception: concludes GDP is useless rather than incomplete

options.text: The Gini coefficient measures inflation, so growth data are wrong.
options.misconception: confuses inequality with price measurement

options.text: Real GDP rose, but the average gain may mask losses for many households.
options.misconception: assumes averages always hide losses without evidence

options.text: Higher Gini implies higher GDP, so welfare clearly improved.
options.misconception: treats inequality as a welfare gain

questions.explanation: Rising real GDP per person can coexist with worsening inequality, meaning the average gain need not reach all households. GDP remains useful but incomplete as a welfare measure.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why output per person can fall despite rising total output
questions.stem: Total real output rises 2% but population rises 3%; what happens to output per person?

options.text: It rises, because total output grew.
options.misconception: ignores population growth in per-capita terms

options.text: It stays flat, because the two effects cancel exactly.
options.misconception: assumes exact cancellation without checking rates

options.text: It falls, because population grew faster than output.
options.misconception: overstates the decline as a collapse

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing prices.
options.misconception: confuses real output with nominal prices

questions.explanation: Output per person equals total output divided by population; if population grows faster, per-person output falls. Prices are already stripped out in real terms.
questions.hint: Compare growth rates of output and population.

questions.stem: GDP is 600 billion, depreciation is 60 billion, and indirect business taxes less subsidies are 30 billion; what is national income?
questions.explanation: National income = GDP - depreciation - (indirect business taxes - subsidies) = 600 - 60 - 30 = 510 billion. Both adjustments remove non-income components.

questions.learningObjective: Explain underground economy bias in GDP
questions.stem: Why does a large underground economy cause measured GDP to understate true output?

options.text: Because underground output is already counted in consumption.
options.misconception: thinks unrecorded activity is captured elsewhere

options.text: Because underground activity is inflationary and raises the deflator.
options.misconception: confuses unrecorded output with price levels

options.text: Because underground wages are included twice in national income.
options.misconception: assumes double counting rather than omission

options.text: Because underground transactions are not recorded in official accounts, so measured output is too low.
options.misconception: overstates the size of the bias as the only error

questions.explanation: Underground transactions escape official recording, so measured GDP understates true production. The bias is an omission, not inflation, double counting, or prior inclusion.

questions.explanation: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M) = 200 + 80 + 60 + 50 - 40 = 350 billion. Imports are subtracted as foreign production.

questions.stem: A firm owned by foreign residents produces output inside the country; which measure counts that output?

options.text: GNP counts it because residents own the firm.
options.misconception: attributes domestic production to resident ownership

options.text: Both GDP and GNP count it equally.
options.misconception: ignores the resident-ownership distinction

options.text: GDP counts it because production occurred within borders.
options.misconception: confuses location with ownership correctly but mislabels

options.text: Neither counts it, since it is foreign-owned.
options.misconception: excludes domestic production from GDP

questions.explanation: GDP measures production within borders regardless of ownership, so foreign-owned domestic output counts in GDP, not GNP. GNP counts output by residents worldwide.
questions.hint: Location defines GDP; ownership defines GNP.

options.text: Disposable personal income, because taxes are already removed.
options.misconception: correctly identifies DPI but misstates the reason

questions.explanation: Disposable personal income is personal income less personal taxes, so it reflects household spending power. Personal income still includes taxes not yet removed.

options.text: Unclear, because GDP omits environmental depreciation and leisure.
options.misconception: correctly notes omission but claims certainty is impossible

options.text: Yes, because timber output exceeds the value of standing forests.
options.misconception: values output flow over natural capital stock

questions.stem: Why is an inventory valuation adjustment added to profits in the income approach?

options.text: To remove the effect of price changes on unsold goods valued at historical cost.
options.misconception: correctly describes the adjustment but overstates its size

options.text: To add the value of goods produced but not yet sold to consumption.
options.misconception: confuses inventory investment with consumption

options.text: To correct for depreciation of capital equipment.
options.misconception: confuses inventory valuation with capital consumption

options.text: To record exports that have not yet shipped.
options.misconception: confuses inventory with export accounting

questions.explanation: Inventory valuation adjustment removes price-change effects from goods held in inventory valued at historical cost. It is not about consumption, depreciation, or exports.

questions.learningObjective: Compute gross domestic income
questions.stem: Wages 300, profits 120, rents 40, interest 30, net indirect taxes 15, and depreciation 60 billion; what is gross domestic income?
questions.explanation: Gross domestic income = wages + profits + rents + interest + net indirect taxes + depreciation = 300 + 120 + 40 + 30 + 15 + 60 = 565 billion.
questions.hint: Sum all income components including depreciation.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute net factor income from GNP and GDP
questions.stem: GNP is 520 billion and GDP is 500 billion; what is net factor income from abroad?
questions.explanation: Net factor income from abroad = GNP - GDP = 520 - 500 = 20 billion. Positive value means residents earn more abroad than foreigners earn domestically.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the personal saving rate
questions.stem: Disposable personal income is 250 billion and personal saving is 25 billion; what is the personal saving rate in percent?
questions.explanation: Personal saving rate = personal saving / disposable personal income * 100 = 25 / 250 * 100 = 10%. It shows the share of after-tax income saved.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Limits of real growth as a welfare measure
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether leisure time is reflected in GDP
questions.stem: A country mandates shorter workweeks; real GDP falls but leisure rises; did welfare fall?

options.text: Yes, because lower GDP always means lower welfare.
options.misconception: treats GDP as a complete welfare measure

options.text: No, because leisure is valuable but excluded from GDP.
options.misconception: correctly notes leisure value but asserts welfare rose

options.text: Yes, because leisure has no market price.
options.misconception: equates no market price with no value

options.text: Uncertain, because GDP omits leisure and the tradeoff is unmeasured.
options.misconception: correctly notes omission and indeterminacy

questions.explanation: GDP excludes leisure, so the measured GDP fall ignores the leisure gain; welfare cannot be judged from GDP alone. The tradeoff is unmeasured.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why productivity drives output per person
questions.stem: What is the main long-run determinant of real output per person?

options.text: The price level, which determines purchasing power.
options.misconception: confuses prices with productive capacity

options.text: Labor productivity, which raises output per worker.
options.misconception: correctly identifies productivity but overstates labor alone

options.text: The nominal interest rate, which stimulates saving.
options.misconception: confuses financial rates with real output

options.text: Government spending, which directly creates output.
options.misconception: overstates fiscal spending as the determinant

questions.explanation: Labor productivity is the main long-run driver of real output per person. Prices, interest rates, and spending are not the fundamental determinants.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the treatment of subsidies in national income
questions.stem: In moving from GDP to national income, how are subsidies treated?

options.text: Subsidies are subtracted, like indirect taxes.
options.misconception: reverses the sign for subsidies

options.text: Subsidies are added, offsetting indirect taxes.
options.misconception: correctly states addition but implies full offset

options.text: Subsidies are ignored entirely.
options.misconception: omits subsidies from the adjustment

options.text: Subsidies are multiplied by the deflator.
options.misconception: confuses subsidies with price adjustment

questions.explanation: Subsidies are added (indirect business taxes are subtracted), so net indirect taxes equal taxes less subsidies. Option B states this; A reverses, C omits, D confuses.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute real GDP growth from nominal and deflator changes
questions.stem: Nominal GDP grew 7% and the deflator grew 3%; what is approximate real GDP growth in percent?
questions.explanation: Real growth ≈ (1.07 / 1.03 - 1) * 100 ≈ 3.88%. Using the simple subtraction gives 4%, close but less precise.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the expenditure approach identity
questions.stem: Which identity defines GDP under the expenditure approach?

options.text: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M).
options.misconception: states the identity but omits the net-export sign convention

options.text: GDP = C + I + G + X + M.
options.misconception: adds imports instead of subtracting them

options.text: GDP = C + I + G - X + M.
options.misconception: reverses exports and imports

options.text: GDP = C + I + G.
options.misconception: omits net exports entirely

questions.explanation: GDP under the expenditure approach equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports (exports minus imports). Option A is correct.
questions.hint: Net exports are exports minus imports.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a country with many foreign-owned factories has GNP below GDP
questions.stem: A country hosts many foreign-owned factories; why is its GNP below its GDP?

options.text: Because GNP excludes all corporate profits.
options.misconception: overstates GNP exclusion

options.text: Because imports exceed exports.
options.misconception: confuses trade balance with factor income

options.text: Because depreciation is higher for foreign firms.
options.misconception: confuses ownership with capital consumption

options.text: Because foreign owners repatriate profits, so resident income is less than domestic output.
options.misconception: correctly explains but implies profits are stolen

questions.explanation: Foreign-owned factories generate domestic output counted in GDP, but their profits accrue to non-residents, so GNP is lower. Trade balance and depreciation do not drive this.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute consumption from DPI and saving
questions.stem: Disposable personal income is 320 billion and the saving rate is 12.5%; what is personal consumption?
questions.explanation: Saving = 320 * 0.125 = 40 billion; consumption = 320 - 40 = 280 billion. Consumption is the complement of saving.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Limits of real growth as a welfare measure
questions.learningObjective: Recognize that GDP ignores resource depletion
questions.stem: A nation pumps oil rapidly; real GDP soars but reserves deplete; is current welfare overstated?

options.text: Yes, because oil prices always fall.
options.misconception: assumes price declines rather than depletion

options.text: No, because oil revenue is income, not capital.
options.misconception: treats resource extraction as pure income

options.text: Yes, because GDP ignores the depreciation of natural capital.
options.misconception: correctly notes omission but asserts overstatement definitively

options.text: No, because reserves are infinite in the long run.
options.misconception: denies resource scarcity

questions.explanation: GDP does not subtract natural capital depreciation, so rapid extraction can overstate sustainable welfare. The measured gain ignores reserve depletion.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why output per person differs from productivity
questions.stem: How does real output per person differ from labor productivity?

options.text: Output per person excludes services; productivity includes them.
options.misconception: misstates sector coverage

options.text: They are identical measures.
options.misconception: ignores denominator differences

options.text: Productivity uses nominal output; per person uses real output.
options.misconception: confuses real/nominal with the denominator

options.text: Output per person divides by total population; productivity divides by workers or hours.
options.misconception: correctly distinguishes denominators but overstates the difference

questions.explanation: Output per person divides by total population, while labor productivity divides by workers or hours. The denominators differ, so the measures differ.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute national income from GNP
questions.stem: GNP is 550 billion, depreciation is 55 billion, and net indirect taxes are 25 billion; what is national income?
questions.explanation: National income = GNP - depreciation - net indirect taxes = 550 - 55 - 25 = 470 billion. Both adjustments remove non-income components.
questions.hint: Subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes from GNP.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how base-year choice affects real GDP
questions.stem: How does the choice of base year affect measured real GDP growth?

options.text: It has no effect, since real GDP removes prices.
options.misconception: ignores weighting in real GDP construction

options.text: It changes relative prices used to weight output, altering growth estimates.
options.misconception: correctly notes weighting but overstates the effect size

options.text: It changes only nominal GDP, not real GDP.
options.misconception: confuses base year with nominal measurement

options.text: It makes real GDP equal to nominal GDP.
options.misconception: equates real and nominal GDP

questions.explanation: Real GDP uses base-year prices to weight output, so the base year affects measured growth through relative price weights. It is not irrelevant or equalizing.

questions.learningObjective: Compute personal income from national income with all adjustments

questions.explanation: Personal income = 600 - 40 - 50 - 10 + 60 = 560 billion. All adjustments convert national income to household-received income.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the residency principle in GNP
questions.stem: What does the residency principle imply for GNP measurement?

options.text: Only citizens are counted as residents.
options.misconception: narrows residency to citizenship

options.text: Output is attributed to the location of production.
options.misconception: confuses residency with territorial principle

options.text: Output is attributed to residents wherever they produce it.
options.misconception: correctly states residency but overstates its ease of measurement

options.text: Foreign workers are always excluded.
options.misconception: excludes resident foreign workers

questions.explanation: GNP attributes output to residents regardless of where production occurs. Location defines GDP, not GNP; residency is not citizenship.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the relationship between DPI and consumption
questions.stem: If disposable personal income rises while the saving rate is constant, what happens to consumption?

options.text: Consumption rises by the same proportion.
options.misconception: assumes exact proportionality without noting MPC

options.text: Consumption falls, since saving absorbs the gain.
options.misconception: confuses higher income with higher saving share

options.text: Consumption is unchanged, since DPI is after-tax.
options.misconception: ignores the income-consumption link

options.text: Consumption rises but by less than DPI, with the rest saved.
options.misconception: correctly notes MPC<1 but overstates the split

questions.explanation: With a constant saving rate, consumption rises with DPI but the marginal propensity to consume is less than one, so part of the gain is saved. Option D captures this.
questions.hint: Not all extra income is spent.

questions.learningObjective: Identify why GDP excludes underground activity
questions.stem: Why is underground activity excluded from official GDP?

options.text: Because it is illegal and therefore worthless.
options.misconception: equates illegality with zero value

options.text: Because it is not reported and thus cannot be measured directly.
options.misconception: correctly states non-reporting but implies it has no value

options.text: Because it is already counted in consumption.

options.text: Because underground activity causes deflation.

questions.explanation: Underground activity is excluded because it is not reported and cannot be measured directly. Its value may still be nonzero.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why chain weighting improves real GDP
questions.stem: Why do national accounts prefer chain-weighted real GDP?

options.text: Because it fixes the base year permanently.
options.misconception: confuses chain weighting with fixed base

options.text: Because it eliminates all price changes.
options.misconception: claims prices are fully removed

options.text: Because it uses average prices across adjacent years, reducing substitution bias.
options.misconception: correctly notes averaging but overstates bias elimination

options.text: Because it measures only consumer goods.
options.misconception: confuses chain weighting with CPI

questions.explanation: Chain weighting uses average prices across adjacent years, reducing substitution bias from a fixed base. It does not eliminate prices, fix the base, or limit scope.
